title: Show HN: Snug – Build an app with Claude, run it with GPT, keep the state
text:
Hi HN,

I've been building software for over 25 years, and something about the way we're building apps with AI has been bothering me.

If Claude builds an app for me today, why shouldn't GPT or a local model be able to run that same app tomorrow?

And if I spend months using that app, who actually owns it, its data, and everything it's learned about how I use it?

We have portable documents, containers, and even models. But the applications we're creating with AI are still largely tied to the environments that created them.

That's what got me working on Snug.

The idea is to separate the application from its intelligence.

A Snug app contains its UI, state, deterministic logic, and a runtime contract. The intelligence comes from the host agent at runtime.

For example, I built a chess app with no chess engine. The app handles the board and UI, while the host AI decides what move to make.

Another example is a personal ledger that can answer questions about your spending without every possible question being hardcoded into the app.

The interesting part is what happens afterward.

Your applications, data, versions, and conversations live in a portable `.snug` file backed by SQLite. The goal is to make it possible to move that application state between compatible hosts without rebuilding everything around a different model.

There are also some important security boundaries: generated apps run in sandboxed iframes, and credentials and network access are mediated by the host rather than handed directly to the app.

I've open-sourced the protocol and reference implementation.

You can try it here:

Playground: https://playground.snugprotocol.org

GitHub: https://github.com/snugprotocol/snug

Specification: https://github.com/snugprotocol/spec

The Playground has a no-key demo mode. The reference implementation also includes Anthropic and OpenAI adapters, a macOS desktop host, and an embeddable runner/SDK.

The spec is at 1.0, but the implementation is still early, and I don't have an ecosystem of independent hosts yet.

I'm not claiming that SQLite, sandboxing, or runtime messaging are new ideas. What I'm exploring is whether combining them around a portable application artifact makes sense as a separate layer for AI-native software.

I'd be interested in feedback from people working on agent runtimes, MCP Apps, and local-first software.

In particular, I'd love to hear where you think this architecture breaks down, or whether there's a simpler way to achieve the same portability.

— Jeetu

I'm David Jeske, the ex-Google acquiree who served as technical architect and engineering director for orkut.com (among other projects) from shortly after the Brazil popularity explosion through the service decline.

I have a few key points to add to this discussion (to the best of my recollection):

1. orkut.com was not acquired. It was developed in-house, the initial version almost entirely written by Orkut Büyükkökten as a 20% time project. It was written in C# .NET as that was what he was most familiar with and efficient in. The actual product launch was championed internally by Marissa Mayer, and encouraged as an experiement in-part because of the external pressure for Google to do "something" in social networking.

2. We believe a huge part of why it became popular in Brazil, was becuase the homepage contained a ranking of users by country and Brazil's national competitive spirit. Brazil made up the largest initial seed network, and once they were #1 on the leaderboards, it became a major viral spread factor in Brazil to "stay on top" of the leaderboard. It was unfortuantly much later in the service that we realized a good portion of why it remained popular only in Brazil was because the service tended to surface the largest sources of activity to users, which meant most users saw significant amounts of Portuguese content. Once we segtregated the service by language, we saw it experience it's second cultural explosion in India.

3. Once we kept up with performance demand on the service, orkut.com fairly quickly grew to serve more daily pages than Google.com websearch (though obviously it was much less complicated as a service, and much less profitable!) However, over time the service became increasingly dominated by abusive usage such as adult images and fake user spamming. orkut.com was always a very small team within Google, as I recall at it's height we had only around 8 engineers on the project as this was very far from Google's core focus at the time. The service ultimately curtailed in popularity as Facebook continued to win markets, including India and Brazil.

4. I believe there was very little connection between orkut.com decline and Google+. By the time Google+ was launched in June 2011, orkut.com was losing ground to Facebook even in Brazil. Facebook overtook orkut.com in Brazil in December 2011, and orkut.com remained online until September 2014, three years after Google+ was launched.

For those curious about technical details:

A. When I became involved in the project, it was because the live service was serving mostly 400 errors and keeling over dead. At the time it was running on Windows and MS-SQL and .NET, the only project of it's kind inside Linux-focused Google. Most of my background is service scalability archicture, so I was asked to get involved to "fix it", I took the team of 5 mostly junior engineers and led the architecture changes to get it serving pages quickly and stop the errors. As I recall, my code-red to fixed the key performance issues took only about a week, after which the massive increase to page performance led to a massive increase in poplarity, causing orkut to shockingly eclipse Google websearch in page views per day not long after.

B. We initially kept the service on .NET technology, both as an experiement within Google, and because I strongly feel the dotnet CLR design (largely due to parametric instantiation and their open-standard model) is the best virtual machine and runtime of it's kind. However, running Windows machines within Google was "not at all straightforward", and it was problematic running on closed source dotnet of the era because we ran into several Microsoft dotnet runtime bugs at scale and had no ability to fix them. We transitioned to using the Mono dotnet runtime on Linux, which was ironically more reliable (and fixable!) and significantly less performant that the Microsoft dotnet runtime for our needs. Eventually the service was transitioned to a Java front-end and C++ backends.

C. Orkut.com images was the first example of Bigtable serving production traffic.

D. We transitioned presentation layer from ASP.NET to Clearsilver templating, developed at my startup Neotonic.com by Brandon Long, and used inside Google for Gmail and other projects. This was for performance, reliability, and to enable the cross platform and cross-language transitions from C# to Java and C++. (Clearsilver was heavily inspired by CS/HDF templating, designed at onelist.com by Scott Shambarger and Ethan Khan) Clearsilver was an unfair weapon in the server-side rendered mostly-static HTML era.
